events_chronological: A screenwriter three months behind on his payments is dodging the finance men who have come for his car.
He pitches a baseball picture at a studio and a young script reader tells the producer to his face that it is flat.
Fleeing the finance men, he blows a tyre and swings into the drive of a crumbling mansion on a famous boulevard.
Mistaken for the undertaker come to collect a dead chimpanzee, he meets a silent-era star nobody has thought about in twenty years.
She hires him to cut down the enormous script she has written as a vehicle for herself.
He moves into the room over the garage, and her butler fetches his belongings from his flat without being asked.
She buys him suits, a cigarette case and a watch, and the arrangement quietly becomes a kept one.
At a New Year party laid on for two she tells him she loves him, and he walks out to a friend's party instead.
The butler telephones to say she has opened her wrists, and he comes back and stays.
He starts slipping out at night to write a script with the young reader, who is engaged to a friend of his.
She drives to the studio with her script; a famous director is gentle with her, and the writer learns the studio only ever wanted to rent her car.
The butler admits that he directed her first pictures, that he was her first husband, and that he has been writing her fan letters himself for years.
She telephones the young reader, and he brings the girl to the house and tells her exactly what he is, so that she will go.
He packs, tells the old star the truth about her career and the letters, and walks out towards the pool.
She shoots him three times and he falls face down into the swimming pool.
With the police and the newsreel cameras filling the hall, she takes them for a film crew and descends the staircase ready for her close-up.
nonlinear_category_reason: Thirteen of fourteen scenes run strictly forward; the one displacement is the shooting, spliced in as the opening image and reached again in the last minutes.
syuzhet_notes: The telling opens on the body floating in the pool and on the dead man's own narration, then rewinds six months and runs forward until it arrives back at the same water. Only that one scene is displaced; everything else is in order.
fabula_notes: The narrator is dead throughout, but the narration is a voice over the action rather than a scene the story is told from, so the body in the pool is a genuine flash-forward rather than a frame.
